title: Preimage of Set Difference under Relation
theorem_text:
Let $\mathcal R \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation.
Let $C$ and $D$ be subsets of $T$.
Then:
$\mathcal R^{-1} \sqbrk C \setminus \mathcal R^{-1} \sqbrk D \subseteq \mathcal R^{-1} \sqbrk {C \setminus D}$
where:
$\setminus$ denotes set difference
$\mathcal R^{-1} \sqbrk C$ denotes the preimage of $C$ under $\mathcal R$.
proof_text:
We have that $\mathcal R^{-1}$ is itself a relation
The result then follows from Image of Set Difference under Relation.
review_reason: Applying the image-of-difference inclusion to the inverse relation gives the stated preimage inclusion with the same direction.

title: Restriction is Subset of Relation
theorem_text:
Let $\mathcal R \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation.
Let $X \subseteq S$.
Then the restriction of $\mathcal R$ to $X$ is a subset of $\mathcal R$.
proof_text:
From the definition of restriction:
$\forall x \in X: \mathcal R \restriction_X \left({x}\right) = \mathcal R \left({x}\right)$
Thus:
$\forall x \in X: \exists t \in T: \left({x, t}\right) \in \mathcal R \restriction_X$
But $\left({x, t}\right)$ is also (by definition) in $\mathcal R$.
It follows that:
$\mathcal R \restriction_X \subseteq \mathcal R$
review_reason: Equality of two fibers does not make them nonempty. A point of X can have no related element in T. The asserted existence fails even for the empty relation.

title: Relation both Symmetric and Asymmetric is Null
theorem_text:
Let $\RR$ be a relation in $S$ which is both symmetric and asymmetric.
Then:
$\RR = \O$
proof_text:
Let $\RR \ne \O$.
Then:
$\exists \tuple {x, y} \in \RR$
Now, either $\tuple {y, x} \in \RR$ or $\tuple {y, x} \notin \RR$.
If $\tuple {y, x} \in \RR$, then $\RR$ is not asymmetric.
If $\tuple {y, x} \notin \RR$, then $\RR$ is not symmetric.
Therefore, if $\RR \ne \O$, $\RR$ can not be both symmetric and asymmetric.
Let $\RR = \O$.
Then:
$\forall x, y \in S: \tuple {x, y} \notin \RR \land \tuple {y, x} \notin \RR$
From Biconditional as Disjunction of Conjunctions:
$\tuple {p \land q} \lor \tuple {\neg p \land \neg q} \vdash p \iff q$
Thus:
$\forall x, y \in S: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR \iff \tuple {y, x} \in \RR$
So the condition for symmetry is fulfilled, and $\RR = \O$ is symmetric.
As $\RR = \O$:
$\forall x, y \in S: \tuple {x, y} \notin \RR$
From False Statement implies Every Statement $\neg p \vdash p \implies q$, we can deduce:
$\forall x, y \in S: \tuple {x, y} \notin \RR$
therefore:
$\forall x, y \in S: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR \implies \forall x, y \in S: \tuple {y, x} \notin \RR$
This is the definition of asymmetric.
Thus the only relation $\RR$ to be both symmetric and asymmetric is $\RR = \O$.
review_reason: A pair in a nonempty relation would require its reverse by symmetry and forbid its reverse by asymmetry. The empty relation satisfies both conditions vacuously.

title: Asymmetric Relation is Antisymmetric
theorem_text:
Let $\RR$ be an asymmetric relation.
Then $\RR$ is also antisymmetric.
proof_text:
Let $\RR$ be asymmetric.
Then from the definition of asymmetric:
$\tuple {x, y} \in \RR \implies \tuple {y, x} \notin \RR$
Thus:
$\neg \exists \tuple {x, y} \in \RR: \tuple {y, x} \in \RR$
Thus:
$\set {\tuple {x, y} \in \RR \land \tuple {y, x} \in \RR} = \O$
Thus:
$\tuple {x, y} \in \RR \land \tuple {y, x} \in \RR \implies x = y$
is vacuously true.
review_reason: Asymmetry rules out mutual relatedness, so the implication from mutual relatedness to equality holds vacuously.

title: Composite Relation with Inverse is Symmetric
theorem_text:
Let $\mathcal R \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation.
Then the composition of $\mathcal R$ with its inverse $\mathcal R^{-1}$ is symmetric:
* $\mathcal R^{-1} \circ \mathcal R$ is a symmetric relation on $S$
* $\mathcal R \circ \mathcal R^{-1}$ is a symmetric relation on $T$.
proof_text:
Note that this result holds for any $\mathcal R \subseteq S \times T$, and does not require that $\left({S, \mathcal R}\right)$ necessarily be a relational structure.
$$\left({a, b}\right) \in \mathcal R^{-1} \circ \mathcal R$$
$$\implies \exists c \in T: \left({a, c}\right) \in \mathcal R \land \left({c, b}\right) \in \mathcal R^{-1}$$
Definition of Composite Relation
$$\implies \exists c \in T: \left({b, c}\right) \in \mathcal R \land \left({c, a}\right) \in \mathcal R^{-1}$$
Definition of Inverse Relation
$$\implies \left({b, a}\right) \in \mathcal R^{-1} \circ \mathcal R$$
Definition of Composite Relation
Thus $\left({a, b}\right) \in \mathcal R^{-1} \circ \mathcal R \implies \left({b, a}\right) \in \mathcal R^{-1} \circ \mathcal R$ and thus $\mathcal R^{-1} \circ \mathcal R$ is symmetric.
As $\mathcal R = \left({\mathcal R^{-1}}\right)^{-1}$ from Inverse of Inverse Relation, it follows that $\mathcal R \circ \mathcal R^{-1} = \left({\mathcal R^{-1}}\right)^{-1} \circ \mathcal R^{-1}$ is likewise a symmetric relation.
The domain of $\mathcal R^{-1} \circ \mathcal R$ is $S$ from Domain of Composite Relation, as is its codomain from Codomain of Composite Relation and the definition of Inverse Relation.
Similarly, the codomain of $\mathcal R \circ \mathcal R^{-1}$ is $T$, as is its domain.
This completes the proof.
review_reason: A common intermediate c works for the reversed pair as well. Replacing the relation by its inverse proves symmetry on T. The extra assertion that every element is in the domain can fail for partial relations, but neither symmetry conclusion relies on it.

title: Equivalence Classes are Disjoint
theorem_text:
Let $\RR$ be an equivalence relation on a set $S$.
Then all $\RR$-classes are pairwise disjoint:
$\tuple {x, y} \notin \RR \iff \eqclass x \RR \cap \eqclass y \RR = \O$
proof_text:
Suppose that for $x, y \in S$:
$\eqclass x {\RR} \cap \eqclass y \RR \ne \O$
Let:
$z \in \eqclass x \RR$
$z \in \eqclass y \RR$
Then by definition of equivalence class:
$\tuple {x, z} \in \RR$
$\tuple {y, z} \in \RR$
Let $c \in \eqclass x \RR$.
That is:
$\tuple {x, c} \in \RR$
By definition of equivalence relation, $\RR$ is symmetric so:
$\tuple {z, x} \in \RR$
By definition of equivalence relation, $\RR$ is transitive so:
$\tuple {z, x} \in \RR \land \tuple {x, c} \in \RR \implies \tuple {z, c} \in \RR$
and
$\tuple {y, z} \in \RR \land \tuple {z, c} \in \RR \implies \tuple {y, c} \in \RR$
So we have $c \in \eqclass y \RR$.
By definition of subset:
$\eqclass x \RR \subseteq \eqclass y \RR$
Similarly, let $c \in \eqclass y \RR$.
That is:
$\tuple {y, c} \in \RR$
By definition of equivalence relation, $\RR$ is symmetric so:
$\tuple {z, y} \in \RR$
By definition of equivalence relation, $\RR$ is transitive so:
$\tuple {z, y} \in \RR \land \tuple {y, c} \in \RR \implies \tuple {z, c} \in \RR$
and
$\tuple {x, z} \in \RR \land \tuple {z, c} \in \RR \implies \tuple {x, c} \in \RR$
So we have $c \in \eqclass x \RR$.
By definition of subset:
$\eqclass y \RR \subseteq \eqclass x \RR$
That is:
$\eqclass x \RR \subseteq \eqclass y \RR$
and
$\eqclass y \RR \subseteq \eqclass x \RR$
By definition of set equality:
$\eqclass x \RR = \eqclass y \RR$
Thus:
$\eqclass x \RR \cap \eqclass y \RR \ne \O \implies \eqclass x \RR = \eqclass y \RR$
and the result follows.
review_reason: A common z and symmetry and transitivity give equality of the two classes. Reflexivity puts each representative in its own class, and related representatives share a member, giving the stated equivalence.

title: Equivalence Class is Unique
theorem_text:
Let $\mathcal R$ be an equivalence relation on $S$.
For each $x \in S$, the one and only one $\mathcal R$-class to which $x$ belongs is $\eqclass x {\mathcal R}$.
proof_text: This follows directly from the Fundamental Theorem on Equivalence Relations: the set of $\mathcal R$-classes forms a partition of $S$.
review_reason: The partition theorem gives exactly one class containing x. Reflexivity identifies that class as the class of x.

title: Intersection of Equivalences
theorem_text: The intersection of two equivalence relations is itself an equivalence relation.
proof_text:
Let $\mathcal R_1$ and $\mathcal R_2$ be equivalence relations on $S$.
Let $\mathcal R_3 = \mathcal R_1 \cap \mathcal R_2$.
Checking in turn each of the criteria for equivalence:
Reflexive
Equivalence relations are by definition reflexive.
So, by Intersection of Reflexive Relations is Reflexive, so is $\mathcal R_3$.
Symmetric
Equivalence relations are by definition symmetric.
So, by Intersection of Symmetric Relations is Symmetric, so is $\mathcal R_3$.
Transitive
Equivalence relations are by definition transitive.
So, by Intersection of Transitive Relations is Transitive, so is $\mathcal R_3$.
Thus $\mathcal R_3$ is an equivalence.
review_reason: Intersecting relations on the same carrier preserves reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity by the three cited closure results.

title: Inverse of Mapping is One-to-Many Relation
theorem_text:
Let $f$ be a mapping.
Then its inverse $f^{-1}$ is a one-to-many relation.
proof_text:
We have that $f$ is a mapping.
Hence $f$ is a fortiori a many-to-one relation.
Then from Inverse of Many-to-One Relation is One-to-Many, $f^{-1}$ is one-to-many.
review_reason: Every function is single-valued, so its inverse is left-unique, the one-to-many property under the terminology used here.

title: Diagonal Relation is Right Identity
theorem_text:
Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation on $S \times T$.
Then:
$\RR \circ \Delta_S = \RR$
where $\Delta_S$ is the diagonal relation on $S$, and $\circ$ signifies composition of relations.
proof_text:
We use the definition of relation equality, as follows:
Equality of Codomains
The codomains of $\RR$ and $\RR \circ \Delta_S$ are both equal to $T$ from Codomain of Composite Relation.
Equality of Domains
The domains of $\RR$ and $\RR \circ \Delta_S$ are also easily shown to be equal.
From Domain of Composite Relation:
$\Dom {\RR \circ \Delta_S} = \Dom {\Delta_S}$
But from the definition of the diagonal relation:
$\Dom {\Delta_S} = \Img {\Delta_S} = S$
Equality of Relations
The composite of $\Delta_S$ and $\RR$ is defined as:
$\RR \circ \Delta_S = \set {\tuple {x, z} \in S \times T: \exists y \in S: \tuple {x, y} \in \Delta_S \land \tuple {y, z} \in \RR}$
But by definition of the diagonal relation on $S$, we have that:
$\tuple {x, y} \in \Delta_S \implies x = y$
Hence:
$\RR \circ \Delta_S = \set {\tuple {y, z} \in S \times T: \exists y \in S: \tuple {y, y} \in \Delta_S \land \tuple {y, z} \in \RR}$
But as $\forall y \in S: \tuple {y, y} \in \Delta_S$, this means:
$\RR \circ \Delta_S = \set {\tuple {y, z} \in S \times T: \tuple {y, z} \in \RR}$
That is:
$\RR \circ \Delta_S = \RR$
Hence the result.
review_reason: The final graph calculation is sufficient: the diagonal forces the intermediate point to equal the first coordinate, leaving exactly the pairs of R. The separate full-domain claim fails for partial relations but is unnecessary.

title: Identity Mapping is Left Identity
theorem_text:
Let $S$ and $T$ be sets.
Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.
Then:
$I_T \circ f = f$
where $I_T$ is the identity mapping on $T$, and $\circ$ signifies composition of mappings.
proof_text:
By definition, a mapping is also a relation.
Also by definition, the identity mapping is the same as the diagonal relation.
Thus Diagonal Relation is Left Identity can be applied directly.
review_reason: The graph of the identity on T is its diagonal, so the cited left-identity law for relations specializes to f.

title: Injection iff Left Inverse
theorem_text:
A mapping $f: S \to T, S \ne \O$ is an injection if and only if:
$\exists g: T \to S: g \circ f = I_S$
where $g$ is a mapping.
That is, if and only if $f$ has a left inverse.
proof_text:
Take the result Condition for Composite Mapping on Left:
Let $A, B, C$ be sets.
Let $f: A \to B$ and $g: A \to C$ be mappings.
Then:
$\forall x, y \in A: \map f x = \map f y \implies \map g x = \map g y$
if and only if:
$\exists h: B \to C$ such that $h$ is a mapping and $h \circ f = g$.
Let $C = A = S$, let $B = T$ and let $g = I_S$.
Then the above translates into:
$\exists h: T \to S$ such that $h$ is a mapping and $h \circ f = g$
if and only if:
$\forall x, y \in S: \map f x = \map f y \implies \map {I_S} x = \map {I_S} y$
But as $\map {I_S} x = x$ and $\map {I_S} y = y$ by definition of identity mapping, it follows that:
$\exists h: T \to S$ such that $h$ is a mapping and $h \circ f = g$
if and only if:
$\forall x, y \in S: \map f x = \map f y \implies x = y$
which is our result.
review_reason: Factoring the identity on S through f requires exactly that equal f-values give equal identity-values, which is injectivity. The nonempty source permits extension outside the image.

title: Injection iff Left Inverse
theorem_text:
A mapping $f: S \to T, S \ne \O$ is an injection if and only if:
$\exists g: T \to S: g \circ f = I_S$
where $g$ is a mapping.
That is, if and only if $f$ has a left inverse.
proof_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be an injection.
Then $f$ is a one-to-many relation.
By Inverse of Many-to-One Relation is One-to-Many, $f^{-1}: T \to S$ is many-to-one.
By Many-to-One Relation Extends to Mapping, there is a Mapping $g: T \to S$ such that $f^{-1} \subseteq g$.
Let $\tuple {x, y} \in g \circ f$.
Then:
$\exists z \in T: \tuple {x, z} \in f, \tuple {z, y} \in g$
Since $\tuple {x, z} \in f$:
$\tuple {z, x} \in f^{-1} \subseteq g$
Since $\tuple {z, y} \in g$, $\tuple {z, x} \in g$ and $g$ is a mapping:
$x = y$
so:
$\tuple {x, y} \in I_S$
So we see that:
$g \circ f \subseteq I_S$
Let $x \in S$.
Then:
$\tuple {x, \map f x} \in f$
and:
$\tuple {\map f x, x} \in f^{-1} \subseteq g$
So:
$\tuple {x, x} \in g \circ f$
Thus:
$I_S \subseteq g \circ f$
By definition of set equality:
$I_S = g \circ f$
review_reason: Starting with an injection, the proof constructs a left inverse and verifies its composite. It never establishes the converse implication from an existing left inverse to injectivity.

title: Restriction of Mapping to Image is Surjection
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.
Let $g: S \to \Img f$ be the restriction of $f$ to $S \times \Img f$.
Then $g$ is a surjective restriction of $f$.
proof_text:
From Image is Subset of Codomain:
$\Img g \subseteq T$
Furthermore, by definition of image, we have:
$\forall s \in S: g \paren s \in \Img g$
Therefore, $g$ may be viewed as a mapping $g: S \to \Img g$.
Thus, by definition, $g$ is a surjection.
review_reason: Restricting the codomain to the image leaves each value unchanged. Consequently the image of g equals the proposed target, and every target element is attained by definition.

title: Surjection iff Right Inverse
theorem_text:
A mapping $f: S \to T, S \ne \O$ is a surjection if and only if:
$\exists g: T \to S: f \circ g = I_T$
where:
$g$ is a mapping
$I_T$ is the identity mapping on $T$.
That is, if and only if $f$ has a right inverse.
proof_text:
Take the result Condition for Composite Mapping on Right:
Let $A, B, C$ be sets.
Let $f: B \to A$ and $g: C \to A$ be mappings.
Then:
$\Img g \subseteq \Img f$
if and only if:
$\exists h: C \to B$ such that $h$ is a mapping and $f \circ h = g$.
Let $C = A = T$, let $B = S$ and let $g = I_T$.
Then the above translates into:
$\Img {I_T} \subseteq \Img f$
if and only if:
$\exists g: T \to S$ such that $g$ is a mapping and $f \circ g = I_T$.
But we know that:
$\Img f \subseteq T = \Img {I_T}$
So by definition of set equality, the result follows.
review_reason: With g the identity on T, the quoted factorization result gives a right inverse exactly when T is contained in the image of f. Together with the reverse inclusion this is surjectivity, under the choice principle implicit in the cited result.

title: Identity Mapping is Bijection
theorem_text: The identity mapping $I_S: S \to S$ on the set $S$ is a bijection.
proof_text:
The identity mapping is:
:an injection, from Identity Mapping is Injection
:a surjection, from Identity Mapping is Surjection
and therefore a bijection.
review_reason: The cited results give both injectivity and surjectivity of the identity on S.

title: Bijection iff Left and Right Inverse
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.
$f$ is a bijection if and only if:
$(1): \quad \exists g_1: T \to S: g_1 \circ f = I_S$
$(2): \quad \exists g_2: T \to S: f \circ g_2 = I_T$
where both $g_1$ and $g_2$ are mappings.
It also follows that it is necessarily the case that $g_1 = g_2$ for such to be possible.
proof_text:
Necessary Condition
Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.
Let $f$ be such that:
$\exists g_1: T \to S: g_1 \circ f = I_S$
$\exists g_2: T \to S: f \circ g_2 = I_T$
where both $g_1$ and $g_2$ are mappings.
Then from Left and Right Inverse Mappings Implies Bijection it follows that $f$ is a bijection.
From Left and Right Inverses of Mapping are Inverse Mapping it follows that:
$g_1 = g_2 = f^{-1}$
where $f^{-1}$ is the inverse of $f$.
Sufficient Condition
Let $f: S \to T$ be a bijection.
Then from Bijection has Left and Right Inverse it follows that:
$f^{-1} \circ f = I_S$ and
$f \circ f^{-1} = I_T$
where $f^{-1}$ is the inverse of $f$.
review_reason: A left and a right inverse force bijectivity and coincide by the cited inverse laws. Conversely the inverse of a bijection satisfies both identities.

title: Inverse of Bijection is Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a bijection in the sense that:
$(1): \quad f$ is an injection
$(2): \quad f$ is a surjection.
Then the inverse $f^{-1}$ of $f$ is itself a bijection by the same definition.
proof_text:
Let $f$ be both an injection and a surjection.
From Mapping is Injection and Surjection iff Inverse is Mapping it follows that its inverse $f^{-1}$ is a mapping.
From Inverse of Inverse Relation:
$\paren {f^{-1} }^{-1} = f$
Thus the inverse of $f^{-1}$ is $f$.
But then $f$, being a bijection, is by definition a mapping.
So from Mapping is Injection and Surjection iff Inverse is Mapping it follows that $f^{-1}$ is a bijection.
review_reason: The inverse relation is a mapping because f is bijective. Its own inverse is f, also a mapping, so the quoted characterization makes the inverse bijective.

title: Inverse Element of Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $S$ and $T$ be sets.
Let $f: S \to T$ be a bijection.
Then:
$\map {f^{-1} } y = x \iff \map f x = y$
where $f^{-1}$ is the inverse mapping of $f$.
proof_text:
Suppose $f$ is a bijection.
Because $f^{-1}$ is a bijection from Bijection iff Inverse is Bijection, it is by definition  a mapping.
The result follows directly from Image of Element under Inverse Mapping.
review_reason: Bijectivity makes the inverse graph a function, and reversing the pair (x,y) identifies its unique value at y as x.

title: Inverse of Inverse of Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a bijection.
Then:
$\paren {f^{-1} }^{-1} = f$
where $f^{-1}$ is the inverse of $f$.
proof_text:
A mapping is a relation.
Thus it follows that Inverse of Inverse Relation can be applied directly.
review_reason: Reversing ordered pairs twice recovers the original relation, which applies to the graph of this bijection.

title: Inverse of Inverse of Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a bijection.
Then:
$\paren {f^{-1} }^{-1} = f$
where $f^{-1}$ is the inverse of $f$.
proof_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a bijection.
From Composite of Bijection with Inverse is Identity Mapping we have:
$f^{-1} \circ f = I_S$
$f \circ f^{-1} = I_T$
where $I_S$ and $I_T$ are the identity mappings on $S$ and $T$ respectively.
The result follows from Left and Right Inverses of Mapping are Inverse Mapping.
review_reason: The two stated composite identities exhibit f as a two-sided inverse of its inverse. Uniqueness gives the claim.

title: Composite of Bijections is Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $f$ and $g$ be mappings such that $\Dom f = \Cdm g$.
Then:
:If $f$ and $g$ are both bijections, then so is $f \circ g$
where $f \circ g$ is the composite mapping of $f$ with $g$.
proof_text:
As every bijection is also by definition an injection, a composite of bijections is also a composite of injections.
Every composite of injections is also an injection by Composite of Injections is Injection.
As every bijection is also by definition a surjection, a composite of bijections is also a composite of surjections.
Every composite of surjections is also a surjection by Composite of Surjections is Surjection.
As a composite of bijections is therefore both an injection and a surjection, it is also a bijection.
review_reason: The compatible composite is injective by composition of injections and surjective by composition of surjections.

title: Composite of Bijections is Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $f$ and $g$ be mappings such that $\Dom f = \Cdm g$.
Then:
:If $f$ and $g$ are both bijections, then so is $f \circ g$
where $f \circ g$ is the composite mapping of $f$ with $g$.
proof_text:
Let $g: X \to Y$ and $f: Y \to Z$ be bijections.
Then from Bijection iff Inverse is Bijection, both $f^{-1}$ and $g^{-1}$ are bijections.
From Inverse of Composite Relation we have that $g^{-1} \circ f^{-1}$ is the inverse of $f \circ g$.
Then:
$\paren {f \circ g} \circ \paren {g^{-1} \circ f^{-1} } = I_Z$
$\paren {g^{-1} \circ f^{-1} } \circ \paren {f \circ g} = I_X$
Hence the result.
review_reason: Reversing the factors gives a mapping from Z to X. Cancelling the two inverse pairs in either composite gives the identity, so the original composite is bijective.

title: Inverse of Composite Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $f$ and $g$ be bijections such that $\Dom g = \Cdm f$.
Then:
$\paren {g \circ f}^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$
and $f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$ is itself a bijection.
proof_text:
$\left({g \circ f}\right)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$ is a specific example of Inverse of Composite Relation.
As $f$ and $g$ are bijections then by Bijection iff Inverse is Bijection, so are both $f^{-1}$ and $g^{-1}$.
By Composite of Bijections is Bijection, it follows that $f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$ is a bijection.
review_reason: The relation-inverse composition rule gives the equality. The two inverse factors are bijections with compatible types, so their composite is bijective.

title: Inverse of Composite Bijection
theorem_text:
Let $f$ and $g$ be bijections such that $\Dom g = \Cdm f$.
Then:
$\paren {g \circ f}^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$
and $f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}$ is itself a bijection.
proof_text:
Let $f: X \to Y$ and $g: Y \to Z$ be bijections.
Then:
$$\paren {g \circ f} \circ \paren {f^{-1} \circ g^{-1} } = g \circ \paren {\paren {f \circ f^{-1} } \circ g^{-1} }$$
Composition of Mappings is Associative
$$= g \circ \paren {I_Y \circ g^{-1} }$$
Composite of Bijection with Inverse is Identity Mapping
$$= g \circ g^{-1}$$
Identity Mapping is Left Identity
$$= I_Z$$
Composite of Bijection with Inverse is Identity Mapping
$$\paren {f^{-1} \circ g^{-1} } \circ \paren {g \circ f} = \paren {f^{-1} \circ \paren {g^{-1} \circ g} } \circ f$$
Composition of Mappings is Associative
$$= \paren {f^{-1} \circ I_Y} \circ f$$
Composite of Bijection with Inverse is Identity Mapping
$$= f^{-1} \circ f$$
Identity Mapping is Right Identity
$$= I_X$$
Composite of Bijection with Inverse is Identity Mapping
Hence the result.
review_reason: The two associative rearrangements yield the identity maps on Z and X. Each composite is therefore the other's two-sided inverse and each is bijective.

title: Composite of Permutations is Permutation
theorem_text:
Let $f, g$ are permutations of a set $S$.
Then their composite $g \circ f$ is also a permutation of $S$.
proof_text:
This follows from the fact that a permutation is a bijection.
The domain and codomain are coincident.
The result follows from Composite of Bijections is Bijection.
review_reason: Both factors are bijections from S to S, so their composite is a bijection with that same source and target.

title: Inverse of Permutation is Permutation
theorem_text: If $f$ is a permutation of $S$, then so is its inverse $f^{-1}$.
proof_text:
Let $f: S \to S$ is a permutation of $S$.
By definition, a permutation is a bijection such that the domain and codomain are the same set.
From Bijection iff Inverse is Bijection, it follows $f^{-1}$ is a bijection.
From the definition of inverse relation, the domain of a relation is the codomain of its inverse and vice versa.
Thus the domain and codomain of $f^{-1}$ are both $S$ and it follows that $f^{-1}$ is a permutation.
review_reason: A bijection of S has an inverse bijection from its target S back to its source S. This is again a permutation.

title: Left Inverse Mapping is Surjection
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be an injection.
Let $g: T \to S$ be a left inverse of $f$.
Then $g$ is a surjection.
proof_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be an injection.
Then from Injection iff Left Inverse there exists at least one left inverse $g: T \to S$ of $f$ such that $g \circ f = I_S$.
$I_S$ is a surjection.
Thus $g \circ f$ is a surjection.
By Surjection if Composite is Surjection it follows that $g$ is also a surjection.
review_reason: For the given left inverse, g composed with f is the surjective identity on S. Hence g reaches every element of S.

title: Right Inverse Mapping is Injection
theorem_text:
Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.
Let $g: T \to S$ be a right inverse of $f$.
Then $g$ is an injection.
proof_text:
By the definition of right inverse:
$f \circ g = I_T$
where $I_T$ is the identity mapping on $T$.
By Identity Mapping is Injection, $I_T$ is an injection.
By Injection if Composite is Injection, it follows that $g$ is an injection.
review_reason: If two g-values agree, applying f gives equal identity-values in T. Thus a right inverse is injective.

title: Image of Union under Mapping
theorem_text:
Let $S$ and $T$ be sets.
Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.
Let $A$ and $B$ be subsets of $S$.
Then:
$f \sqbrk {A \cup B} = f \sqbrk A \cup f \sqbrk B$
This can be expressed in the language and notation of direct image mappings as:
$\forall A, B \in \powerset S: \map {f^\to} {A \cup B} = \map {f^\to} A \cup \map {f^\to} B$
proof_text:
As $f$, being a mapping, is also a relation, we can apply Image of Union under Relation:
$\RR \sqbrk {A \cup B} = \RR \sqbrk A \cup \RR \sqbrk B$
review_reason: Treating the graph of f as the relation in the cited union identity gives exactly the two image formulas.
